entities.label: Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio
entities.sub: USAF installation, Greene and Montgomery Counties, Ohio; AFMC and NASIC host site
entities.desc: Wright-Patterson Air Force Base sits immediately east and northeast of Dayton, Ohio, straddling Greene and Montgomery Counties, and was formally constituted on 13 January 1948 by consolidating Wright Field, Patterson Field, Dayton Army Air Field and Clinton Army Air Field into a single installation. Wright Field had been a flying field since 22 May 1917; Patterson Field was named on 1 July 1931 for Lt. Frank Stuart Patterson. The base's significance to this board is not its size but its function: from 1945 onward it was the address of American foreign materiel exploitation. The Air Materiel Command T-2 intelligence organisation here received the Operation Paperclip haul; T-2 became the Air Technical Intelligence Center in 1951, ATIC became the Foreign Technology Division in 1961, FTD became the Foreign Aerospace Science and Technology Center in 1991 and then the National Air and Space Intelligence Center in 1993, which is still headquartered here. Every official Air Force UFO project - SIGN (1948), GRUDGE (1949) and Blue Book (1952-1969) - was hosted at this base, under the command that dismantles recovered foreign hardware, not under a science agency or an air defence command. Lt. Gen. Nathan Twining wrote the 23 September 1947 'AMC Opinion Concerning Flying Discs' as commander of Air Materiel Command here; Col. Howard McCoy ran T-2 intelligence here; Capt. Edward Ruppelt ran Blue Book here; J. Allen Hynek consulted here. The 1969 Bolender memo, written by Brig. Gen. Carroll Bolender, closed Blue Book while stating that reports 'which could affect national security' were never part of the Blue Book system - a sentence written about this base's own reporting architecture. 'Hangar 18' in Area B is the popular name attached since at least the 1970s to the alleged storage of Roswell material here; no primary record establishes such storage, and the persistent structural fact is more damning than the folklore: the base's 1947-1951 T-2 intelligence files have never undergone a comprehensive declassification review, and NASIC remains the institutional heir with continuous custody of the filing system. In wave 1 the pseudonymous NASIC-affiliated source 'Jonathan Grey' is placed here.

entities.label: Kirtland Air Force Base and Albuquerque, New Mexico
entities.sub: 51,558-acre USAF installation, southeast Albuquerque; AFRL Directed Energy, AFNWC, Manzano, KUMMSC, Sandia
entities.desc: Kirtland Air Force Base occupies 51,558 acres in the southeast quadrant of Albuquerque, sharing runways with the Albuquerque International Sunport. It began as three private airfields, was taken over as Albuquerque Army Air Base in 1941, renamed Kirtland Army Air Field on 24 February 1942 for Col. Roy C. Kirtland, and became Kirtland Air Force Base on 13 January 1948 - the same day as Wright-Patterson. Its relevance is that it is the single densest concentration of nuclear-weapons and directed-energy infrastructure in the United States sitting inside a city: Sandia National Laboratories, descended from the Manhattan Project's Z Division, is adjacent; the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center and the 377th Air Base Wing are hosted here; the Air Force Research Laboratory Directed Energy Directorate runs the laser and high-power microwave portfolio here; the Manzano Base weapons storage complex, tunnelled into the Manzano Mountains on the base's eastern edge, merged administratively with Kirtland on 1 July 1971; and the Kirtland Underground Munitions Maintenance and Storage Complex, activated in 1992, is described in the base's own literature as the largest nuclear weapons storage facility in the world, with more than 300,000 square feet underground. Kirtland is also the operational address of the best-documented domestic UAP-adjacent counterintelligence operation on the record. Albuquerque businessman Paul Bennewitz, whose company Thunder Scientific sat on the base perimeter and sold humidity sensors licensed from Sandia in 1966, began a self-funded study in July 1979, filmed lights over the Manzano storage area and recorded anomalous signals, contacted the base on 24 October 1980 and briefed Kirtland officials on 10 November 1980. What followed was a sustained feed of fabricated material through the Air Force Office of Special Investigations detachment here, later admitted in public by AFOSI special agent Richard C. Doty and by UFO researcher William Moore, who stated on 1 July 1989 that he had participated in an effort to push Bennewitz toward a breakdown by feeding him false information. Bennewitz was hospitalised in August 1988 and died on 23 June 2003. The Bennewitz operation is the board's clearest evidence that counterintelligence resources were deployed against a private citizen over UAP-adjacent observations at a nuclear site, and Kirtland is where it happened.

entities.label: Roswell, New Mexico and the Foster Ranch, Lincoln County
entities.sub: City in Chaves County; site of Roswell Army Air Field, home of the 509th Bomb Group; debris field ~75 mi NW near Corona
entities.desc: Roswell is a city in Chaves County in southeastern New Mexico, and in 1947 it was the home of Roswell Army Air Field and the 509th Bomb Group - at that moment the only atomic-capable bomb group in the world, the unit that had dropped the weapons on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. That single fact governs everything about the site's significance: whatever came down on the Foster Ranch, roughly seventy-five miles northwest near Corona in Lincoln County, came down inside the security envelope of the only nuclear strike force on Earth, and the recovery was executed by that force's own intelligence office. Rancher W. W. 'Mac' Brazel found debris in late June 1947, reported it to Chaves County Sheriff George Wilcox on 6 July, and RAAF sent Maj. Jesse Marcel, the 509th's intelligence officer, and Capt. Sheridan Cavitt of the Counter Intelligence Corps to retrieve it. On 8 July 1947 the base public information officer, 1st Lt. Walter Haut, issued a press release stating that 'the intelligence office of the 509th Bomb group of the Eighth Air Force, Roswell Army Air Field, was fortunate enough to gain possession of a disc.' Within hours Brig. Gen. Roger M. Ramey, commanding Eighth Air Force at Fort Worth Army Air Field, retracted it in front of press photographers with weather officer Warrant Officer Irving Newton, presenting the material as a weather balloon and radar target. The Air Force's own two later reports - the 1994 report identifying the debris as Project Mogul Flight No. 4 balloon train material launched from Alamogordo, and 'The Roswell Report: Case Closed' of 24 June 1997 attributing body reports to anthropomorphic parachute test dummies - concede the central structural point: the 1947 statement was a cover story, issued by the Army Air Forces, to protect a classified programme. What Roswell demonstrates for this board is therefore not settled by the debris identification. It is that the United States has admitted, in its own official reports, to fabricating a public explanation for a materiel recovery in 1947, and that when GAO audited the paper trail in 1995 it found that RAAF outgoing messages for October 1946 to December 1949 had been destroyed with no disposition authority located. The record of the recovery was removed. That is the fact that survives audit.

entities.label: Groom Lake, Nevada
entities.sub: Dry lakebed and USAF/CIA flight test facility, Lincoln County, Nevada; R-4808N; 83 mi NNW of Las Vegas
entities.desc: Groom Lake is a salt flat roughly 3.75 miles north-south by 3 miles east-west at about 4,409 feet elevation in the Groom Lake Valley of Lincoln County, Nevada, 83 miles north-northwest of Las Vegas and 25 miles south of Rachel. The flight test facility on its southwest shore sits inside Restricted Area 4808 North, the 'Groom box' - a 23-by-25-mile block of restricted airspace enclosing the original 6-by-10-mile rectangular withdrawal - and abuts Yucca Flat, where 739 of the 928 Nevada Test Site nuclear detonations occurred. Its acknowledgement history is the reason it belongs on this board as a case study in how the United States conceals a physical installation for decades and then concedes it in fragments. The CIA established the site in April 1955 for Project AQUATONE, the U-2; the first U-2 arrived on 24 July 1955. Project OXCART, the A-12, was established in August 1959, construction of the 8,500-foot runway began in September 1960, the first A-12 arrived 28 February 1962 and flew on 26 April 1962. HAVE BLUE, the Lockheed stealth demonstrator, first flew here in December 1977; the YF-117A first flew on 18 June 1981 with Lockheed test pilot Hal Farley; Northrop's TACIT BLUE first flew 5 February 1982 with Richard G. Thomas. Exploited foreign aircraft were flown here from the late 1960s under HAVE DOUGHNUT, HAVE DRILL, HAVE IDEA and HAVE GLIB. Against that record, the government's disclosure posture is instructive: no acknowledgement of any kind until 1995, when President Clinton issued a presidential determination exempting 'the Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake, Nevada' from environmental disclosure laws - a determination reissued annually since - which arose out of Kasza v. Browner and Frost v. Perry, the 1994 suits by contractors and by the widows of Walter Kasza and Robert Frost alleging exposure to chemicals burned in open pits, in which Rutgers biochemists found elevated dioxin, dibenzofuran and trichloroethylene in claimants' body fat. District Judge Philip Pro rejected the state secrets claim; the suits were dismissed for lack of evidence; the Ninth Circuit affirmed; the Supreme Court declined review. The Air Force acknowledged the site's existence in 1998. Only on 25 June 2013, answering a 2005 FOIA request by Jeffrey T. Richelson of the National Security Archive, did the CIA release the U-2 and OXCART history naming Area 51 and admitting specific activity there. That is fifty-eight years from establishment to specific acknowledgement, achieved by FOIA litigation rather than by voluntary disclosure - the template against which every current UAP disclosure claim should be measured. The cover story function matters too: Groom's own historians note the U-2's high-altitude operations generated a wave of civilian UFO reports in the late 1950s that the Air Force did not correct, meaning a real black programme was knowingly allowed to be absorbed into the UFO explanation space.

entities.label: Area 51 (Homey Airport / Groom Lake operating location)
entities.sub: Named USAF/CIA facility at Groom Lake; KXTA / Homey Airport; part of the Nevada Test and Training Range
entities.desc: 'Area 51' is the name attached to the operating facility on the southwest shore of Groom Lake, carried on aeronautical charts as Homey Airport (KXTA) and administratively part of the Nevada Test and Training Range. It is treated here as a distinct node from the lakebed itself because the name, rather than the geography, is what carries the evidentiary weight: it is the name the CIA finally used in the 25 June 2013 release, the name in the 1995 presidential environmental determination's careful circumlocution ('the Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake, Nevada'), and the name around which the entire modern reverse-engineering claim structure was built. In May 1989 Robert Lazar told KLAS-TV reporter George Knapp in Las Vegas that he had been contracted to work on craft of non-human origin at 'S-4', a facility he placed underground in the Papoose Range near Papoose Lake, about 8.5 miles south of the main base. Lazar's account is the origin point of the public reverse-engineering narrative and remains uncorroborated by any primary record; it is also the reason that, for thirty-seven years, the phrase 'Area 51' has functioned as a container that absorbs and discredits serious custody claims. The board's position is that the two things are separable. The documented reality of Area 51 - a facility whose existence the government refused to concede for four decades while flying AQUATONE, OXCART, HAVE BLUE, TACIT BLUE and exploited Soviet airframes out of it - is itself proof of the state's capacity and willingness to run large, physically substantial, contractor-staffed programmes entirely outside the acknowledged record. That capacity is the load-bearing claim. Lazar's specific allegations are not required to support it and are recorded separately at their own evidentiary grade.

entities.sub: Sandia-operated test range and USAF airfield, Nye County, Nevada; F-117 operational basing 1982-1992
entities.desc: The Tonopah Test Range occupies the northwest corner of the Nevada Test and Training Range in Nye County, is operated for the Department of Energy by Sandia National Laboratories for weapons ballistics and delivery testing, and hosts a USAF airfield that served as the operational base of the F-117A programme. Whitley Jr. became the first USAF pilot to fly the F-117A on 15 October 1982. HAVE IDEA, the exploited-foreign-aircraft programme, transitioned from Groom to Tonopah in May 1973. The F-117 was not acknowledged until November 1988. What Tonopah proves is that the United States has demonstrably concealed not merely a technology but an entire manned operational flying unit, with its own base, its own night-only flying schedule and its own commuter airline out of Las Vegas, for six years after it entered service - which is the correct scale reference for evaluating claims about a concealed materiel exploitation programme with a contractor workforce.

entities.label: White Sands Missile Range, New Mexico
entities.sub: ~3,200 sq mi Army range across five New Mexico counties; Trinity Site; V-2 launch complex
entities.desc: White Sands Missile Range covers almost 3,200 square miles across Dona Ana, Otero, Socorro, Sierra and Lincoln Counties in New Mexico, making it the largest military installation in the United States. It was established as White Sands Proving Ground on 9 July 1945; seven days later, on 16 July 1945, the first atomic detonation took place at Trinity Site near its northern boundary. After the war 100 captured German V-2 rockets were shipped here and 67 were fired between 1946 and 1951; by 1946 thirty-five Operation Paperclip scientists were working at the proving ground. This is the geographic centre of everything that matters about 1947-1950 in New Mexico: Trinity, the V-2 programme, the Paperclip cohort, Los Alamos to the north, Sandia and Kirtland to the northwest, Alamogordo and the Project Mogul launch site to the east, and the Foster Ranch debris field to the northeast. The range is also the origin of the most technically interesting early observational record in the American file. From 1948 the Land-Air Inc. optical tracking crews - professional cinetheodolite operators whose entire job was measuring the trajectories of fast objects - reported unidentified objects on the range, and it was these observations, together with the green fireball reports over the Los Alamos and Sandia corridor, that produced the 16 February 1949 Los Alamos conference attended by Edward Teller and the Air Force's Project Twinkle instrumented observation effort at Holloman and Vaughn, New Mexico, from 1950. The significance is that the earliest instrumented, professional-observer UAP reporting in the United States came from inside the nuclear weapons and rocketry complex, gathered by people employed to measure objects in flight, and it was answered with a small, underfunded, quietly terminated camera project rather than a serious collection programme.

entities.desc: Los Alamos sits on the Pajarito Plateau in Los Alamos County, New Mexico, and is the site of the laboratory established in 1943 as Project Y of the Manhattan Project, now Los Alamos National Laboratory. Its place on this board rests on two things. First, it is one of the two nuclear design laboratories and therefore one of the small number of American institutions with both the compartmentation architecture and the materials-science capability that a concealed exploitation programme would require; whistleblower accounts collected by AAWSAP and by David Grusch describe materials work distributed across the Department of Energy laboratory complex and its industrial partners, and no document has been produced placing any specific laboratory inside such a programme. LANL's own published account records that the phenomenon was ultimately dismissed as a national security threat, a conclusion that did not prevent the Air Force from standing up Project Twinkle ten months later to instrument it. Los Alamos is thus the first place where American nuclear scientists formally met to discuss unexplained objects over their own facilities, and the meeting is on the laboratory's own record.

entities.sub: 470 sq mi USAF flight test centre on Rogers Dry Lake, Kern County; AFTC, USAF Test Pilot School, NASA Armstrong
entities.desc: Edwards Air Force Base covers 470 square miles of the western Mojave in Kern County, California, built around Rogers Dry Lake, an endorheic salt pan whose hard surface functions as a natural extension of the runways. It began in 1933 as the Muroc Bombing and Gunnery Range and was renamed in December 1949 for Capt. Glen Edwards, killed in the crash of the Northrop YB-49 flying wing. It hosts the Air Force Test Center, the U.S. Air Force Test Pilot School and NASA's Armstrong Flight Research Center. Edwards is the acknowledged, white-world twin of Groom Lake: it is where American aircraft are flight tested when the government intends to admit they exist. That relationship is itself evidentiary. The CIA's own explanation for selecting Groom Lake in 1955 was explicit - flight test and pilot training for the U-2 could not be conducted at Edwards or at Lockheed's Palmdale facility given the extreme secrecy of the project. Edwards therefore defines the boundary condition: everything the United States is willing to acknowledge flies here, and the existence of a parallel unacknowledged test enterprise is established by the documented decision to move work away from this base. Edwards is also attached to one of the oldest and least substantiated claims in the field, the alleged February 1954 Muroc meeting between President Eisenhower and non-human occupants; the board records that claim as folklore with no primary record, and notes that its persistence has been useful to the concealment insofar as it makes the base's genuinely documented role harder to discuss seriously.

entities.desc: Boulder is where the United States government purchased the scientific verdict that closed the UFO question for a generation. In October 1966 the Air Force announced a contract with the University of Colorado at Boulder for an independent scientific study of unidentified flying objects, initially funded at $313,000 and eventually exceeding $500,000, directed by the physicist Edward U. Condon with Robert J. Low as coordinator. The project's integrity collapsed in public when James E. McDonald found in the project files, in July 1967, Low's internal memorandum of 9 August 1966 to university administrators proposing that the study be 'conducted almost entirely by non-believers' and present 'the image of a group of non-believers trying their best to be objective but having an almost zero expectation of finding a saucer.' David Saunders and Norman Levine were dismissed; litigation was threatened in both directions. The 1,485-page report was delivered to the Air Force in November 1968 and released publicly in January 1969, concluding that 'nothing has come from the study of UFOs in the past 21 years that has added to scientific knowledge.' A National Academy of Sciences panel chaired by Gerald M. Clemence endorsed it. On 17 December 1969 the Air Force terminated Project Blue Book, citing the Condon findings. Boulder therefore represents the mechanism this board is most concerned with after outright classification: a government agency funding an ostensibly independent academic body whose internal correspondence shows the conclusion was framed in advance, and then using that body's report as the legal and public justification for shutting down its own reporting channel. The Bolender memo of the same period establishes that reports affecting national security were never in Blue Book to begin with - which means the channel that was closed at Boulder's recommendation was not the channel that mattered.

entities.label: USS Nimitz Carrier Strike Group Encounters, 10-16 November 2004
entities.sub: Multi-platform radar/visual/infrared UAP encounters, Southern California Operating Area; the 'Tic Tac'
entities.desc: Between roughly 10 and 16 November 2004 the Nimitz Carrier Strike Group, working up off southern California in the W-291 warning area and the Baja approaches, generated the most completely corroborated UAP encounter in the American record: radar, multiple aircrew eyewitnesses, and an infrared recording, on separate platforms, inside a controlled military exercise area. The guided-missile cruiser USS Princeton (CG-59), running a freshly upgraded SPY-1B, had been holding anomalous tracks on its Aegis combat system for approximately two weeks; Senior Chief Operations Specialist Kevin Day ran the air picture. Fravor's sworn statement to House Oversight describes the objects descending from above 80,000 feet 'rapidly down to 20,000ft', loitering for hours, then ascending. On 14 November 2004 Princeton vectored two VFA-41 Black Aces F/A-18Fs off a training event to a contact. Cdr. David Fravor, the squadron's commanding officer, and his weapons systems officer flew the lead; Lt. Cdr. Alex Dietrich and her WSO flew high cover from about 8,000 feet above. Fravor found a small white object, no rotors, no rotor wash, no visible control surfaces, moving erratically over an area of white water in an otherwise calm sea, its long axis initially north-south. Four aircrew watched it for roughly five minutes. As Fravor descended in a spiral to intercept, the object mirrored his turn, then accelerated out of sight; Princeton reacquired it at the CAP point roughly 60 miles away in under a minute. A follow-on sortie that day, flown with a functioning ATFLIR pod and credited to Lt. Cdr. Chad Underwood, produced the infrared footage now known as FLIR1 - the video that leaked in 2007, was published by The New York Times on 16 December 2017, and was formally released by the Department of Defense on 27 April 2020 with the statement that the phenomena 'remain characterized as unidentified.' What happened afterwards is the part that matters institutionally. The Navy's own range fouler report on the incident, released to the Navy FOIA reading room on 12 January 2023, describes the object as 'solid white, smooth, with no edges ... uniformly colored with no nacelles, pylons, or wings ... approximately 46 feet in length', names Fravor and Dietrich, and records the disposition in one sentence: 'Pilots reported the incident through Intelligence Personnel. Reporting terminated at 3rd Fleet, there was no process to share the reporting.' Fravor testified under oath on 26 July 2023 that 'the incident was never investigated, none of my crew were ever questioned, tapes were never taken.' Against that, three USS Princeton crewmen in different divisions - Kevin Day, CEC/Aegis technician Gary Voorhis and Jason Turner - have described in public interviews since 2018 that within roughly 48 hours personnel who did not identify themselves came aboard and removed or ordered wiped the recording media covering the tracks, and that crew were told to stop discussing it. No FOIA release, visit log, deck-log entry or message traffic has ever been produced identifying those personnel or the authority under which they acted, and the Navy has never produced Princeton sensor data for 14 November 2004. The two accounts are not necessarily in conflict - Fravor speaks for the aircrew and the squadron's tapes, the Princeton crew speak for the ship's recorded data - but the confiscation account remains the single most consequential unanchored claim in the modern record, and it is graded here as an inference, not a fact.

entities.label: Immaculate Constellation disclosure, October-November 2024
entities.sub: Alleged unacknowledged SAP; 12-page report delivered by Shellenberger and entered into the Congressional Record 13 Nov 2024
entities.desc: Immaculate Constellation is the name of an alleged unacknowledged special access program that entered the public record in October 2024 through the journalist Michael Shellenberger and entered the Congressional Record on 13 November 2024. Shellenberger, founder of Public, reported that a current or former US government official acting as a UAP whistleblower had provided him a report; the source told Public the programme is 'a strategic intelligence program', and a former intelligence community official subsequently confirmed its existence to him. Shellenberger's written testimony to the House Oversight Committee states the whistleblower alleges the Department of Defense created the programme in 2017 after the New York Times published on AATIP, and that a source subsequently told him it 'is controlled by the White House and executed and administrated by the DOD to avoid compliance with Title 10' - which is a specific, testable allegation about the legal mechanism of concealment, not a vague assertion of secrecy. The twelve-page document has two sections: the first describing the USAP, the second concerning US Government imagery intelligence. Under oath Shellenberger characterised Immaculate Constellation as serving 'as a central or parent USAP that consolidates observations of UAPs by both tasked and untasked collection platforms', holding 'high-quality imagery intelligence and measurement and signature intelligence' drawn from low Earth orbit, the upper atmosphere, aviation altitudes and maritime environments, across infrared, forward-looking infrared, full motion video and still photography. The report catalogues recurring morphologies observed from 1991 to 2022 - spheres and orbs, discs and saucers, ovals and tic-tacs, triangles, boomerang and arrowhead forms, and irregular or organic shapes - and describes specific incidents: 'orbs surrounding and forcing an F-22 out of its patrol area'; 'the crew of a Navy aircraft carrier watched a small orange/red sphere rapidly descend from a high altitude of 100 to 200 yards directly above the flight deck'; and 'a roughly 13-minute long, high-definition, full-color video of a white orb UAP coming out of the ocean approximately 20 miles off the coast of Kuwait ... joined by another orb that briefly comes into the frame from the left.' Under questioning from Rep. Clay Higgins, Shellenberger confirmed 'I do' know the author, and refused to place his sources: 'I will not say ... I protect my sources, and I am not willing to reduce the potential universe of where my sources might be.' Chairwoman Nancy Mace then moved the document into the record: 'Committee staff asked me to go ahead, and I will do it, to enter into the Congressional Record this 12-page document that Michael Shellenberger brought today that describes the Immaculate Constellation government program.' It appears in the hearing's Index of Documents as 'Report, Pentagon, Immaculate Constellation; submitted by Rep. Mace.' The official response is the important part of this dossier. The Department of Defense says it has no record of such a programme; Pentagon spokesperson Sue Gough has stated the Department has 'no record'; former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick has denied it exists. No AARO product has ever addressed it: not the FY2024 annual report, not the FY2025 report delivered 21 July 2026, not any statement for the record, and no PURSUE tranche between 8 May and 7 August 2026 released anything under the name. In 2025 a self-identified whistleblower said he had located the material in a folder labelled '2018 Schriever Wargame', and Jason Colavito assessed that the claimant had mistaken fictitious wargame documents for secret UFO revelations - an assessment that, whatever its merits, addresses a later claimant's provenance story and not Shellenberger's source. The board's position is that the load-bearing fact is procedural: a named programme is in the Congressional Record, the Department's answer is a records assertion rather than a denial of existence, and in the twenty-one months since no office has produced a written response, a records search declaration, or a classification review.

entities.label: Roswell Incident, June-July 1947
entities.sub: Materiel recovery near Corona, NM; RAAF 'flying disc' press release 8 July 1947 and same-day retraction
entities.desc: In late June 1947 rancher W. W. 'Mac' Brazel found debris scattered on the Foster Ranch near Corona, in Lincoln County, New Mexico, roughly seventy-five miles northwest of Roswell. On 6 July he reported it to Chaves County Sheriff George Wilcox, who called Roswell Army Air Field. RAAF dispatched Maj. Jesse A. Marcel Sr., intelligence officer of the 509th Bomb Group - at that date the only nuclear-capable bomb group in existence - and Capt. Sheridan Cavitt of the Counter Intelligence Corps. On 8 July 1947 the base public information officer, 1st Lt. Walter Haut, issued a press release stating that 'the intelligence office of the 509th Bomb group of the Eighth Air Force, Roswell Army Air Field, was fortunate enough to gain possession of a disc.' The story went out on the wires within hours. That same day Brig. Gen. Roger M. Ramey, commanding Eighth Air Force at Fort Worth Army Air Field, staged a press conference with weather officer Warrant Officer Irving Newton and presented the material as a weather balloon and a radar target reflector. The Air Force's own subsequent reports concede the essential structure: the 1994 report identified the debris as a Project Mogul balloon train, specifically Flight No. 4 launched 4 June 1947 from Alamogordo Army Air Field, and explicitly acknowledged that the weather balloon statement had been a cover story to divert attention from a classified programme; 'The Roswell Report: Case Closed', published 24 June 1997 and authored in part by declassification officer 1st Lt. James McAndrew, attributed accounts of recovered bodies to anthropomorphic parachute test dummies dropped in 1950s high-altitude programmes. Roswell's evidentiary value to this board does not depend on adjudicating what the debris was. It rests on two documented facts. First, the United States has conceded in writing that it issued a false public explanation for a materiel recovery in 1947. Second, when Rep. Steven H. Schiff asked GAO to audit the paper trail after the Defense Department declined to answer him, GAO/NSIAD-95-187 reported that RAAF outgoing messages from October 1946 through December 1949 had been destroyed and that no disposition authority for the destruction could be located. The unit's message traffic for the period covering the recovery no longer exists, and nobody has ever produced the authority that ordered it destroyed. That finding has never been rebutted by any agency.

entities.label: STAR GATE and predecessor remote viewing programs, 1970-1995
entities.sub: CIA/Army/DIA psychoenergetics effort; SCANATE, GONDOLA WISH, GRILL FLAME, CENTER LANE, SUN STREAK, STAR GATE
entities.desc: STAR GATE is the umbrella name applied in 1991 to a chain of United States government programmes investigating and attempting to operationalise remote viewing, running from 1970 to 1995 across CIA, Army and DIA sponsorship. The CIA initiated SCANATE - 'scan by coordinate' - around 1970 in response to assessments that the Soviet Union was spending heavily on psychotronic research. In 1972 physicists Harold E. Puthoff and Russell Targ began CIA-sponsored work at SRI International's Artificial Intelligence Center in Menlo Park, coining the term 'remote viewing' and working with Ingo Swann, Pat Price, Joseph McMoneagle and Uri Geller. The military side began as GONDOLA WISH in 1977 under the Army Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence's Systems Exploitation Detachment, became GRILL FLAME under INSCOM in mid-1978 in Buildings 2560-2561 at Fort Meade, was redesignated CENTER LANE in 1983, moved to DIA's Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate as SUN STREAK in late 1985, and was consolidated as STAR GATE in 1991. Maj. Gen. Albert Stubblebine sponsored the Fort Meade effort; Lt. Frederick 'Skip' Atwater oversaw the unit until 1987; James Clapper, later Director of National Intelligence, led the project in the 1990s; Edwin C. May ran the Cognitive Sciences Laboratory as principal investigator. In 1995 CIA commissioned the American Institutes for Research to evaluate the programme; statistician Jessica Utts concluded the laboratory results showed statistically significant effects, psychologist Ray Hyman concluded the opposite - 'the overwhelming amount of data generated by the viewers is vague, general, and way off target' - and the official finding was that remote viewing information 'is vague and ambiguous, making it difficult, if not impossible, for the technique to yield information of sufficient quality and accuracy for actionable intelligence.' CIA terminated the roughly $20 million programme in 1995 and published the records online in January 2017 through the CREST archive; Edwin May's donated 1972-1995 materials are held at the Archives of the Impossible at Rice University. STAR GATE belongs on this board for four reasons and only four. It is a documented case of the United States funding two decades of research into a phenomenon it publicly disparaged. It shows the exact contractor structure a concealed programme uses - a university-adjacent institute holding the science, a compartmented military unit holding the operations, and an intelligence sponsor holding the money. It establishes the personnel bridge that runs through Puthoff from SRI to EarthTech to the AAWSAP Defense Intelligence Reference Documents to To The Stars Academy and the 2019 Army CRADA, and through Christopher 'Kit' Green from the CIA weird desk to NIDS-adjacent biomedical work. And it is the precedent for how such a programme ends: not with a public admission, but with a commissioned evaluation that produces an unusable-for-intelligence finding, followed by termination and, twenty-two years later, bulk declassification.

entities.label: New York Times, 'Glowing Auras and Black Money', 16 December 2017
entities.sub: Publication revealing AATIP, the $22m appropriation, Elizondo's resignation and two Navy videos
entities.desc: On 16 December 2017 The New York Times published 'Glowing Auras and Black Money: The Pentagon's Mysterious U.F.O. Program' by Helene Cooper, Ralph Blumenthal and Leslie Kean, together with a companion piece by Bryan Bender in Politico. The story disclosed the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program; a roughly $22 million appropriation over five years from 2007 to 2012 arranged by Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid at the urging of Nevada businessman Robert Bigelow, most of which went to Bigelow's company; Luis Elizondo's role and his resignation letter protesting excessive secrecy and internal opposition; and two Navy infrared targeting-pod videos, including the November 2004 Nimitz footage. Pentagon spokeswoman Dana White confirmed to Politico that Elizondo had directed AATIP; officials confirmed the programme's existence while disputing its significance, and an anonymous former congressional staffer said 'after all of that there was really nothing there that we could find.' The Times also carried scepticism from James Oberg and Sara Seager. The board records this as the pivotal event of the modern era, and records precisely why: the story added no new physical evidence about any object. What it added was institutional standing. Nancy Mace under oath has never been produced publicly. The hearing established the subject as legitimate congressional business and simultaneously demonstrated the limits of a committee without jurisdiction over the compartments it is asking about.

entities.desc: On 9 September 2025 at 10:00 am in HVC-210 the House Oversight Committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna with Rep. Jasmine Crockett as ranking member, held 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection'. The witnesses were Jeffrey Nuccetelli, a sixteen-year Air Force veteran who served in security forces at Vandenberg; Senior Chief Petty Officer Alexandro C. Wiggins, an operations specialist aboard USS Jackson (LCS-6); the journalist George Knapp; Dylan Borland, a former Air Force geospatial intelligence specialist; and, as minority witness, Joe Spielberger, senior policy counsel at the Project On Government Oversight. This is the hinge hearing of the modern era because it moved the enquiry from the phenomenon to the machinery. Nuccetelli testified to the 14 October 2003 Vandenberg incidents over missile defence sites, said each incident was 'witnessed by multiple personnel, documented, investigated and reported up the chain of command', stated that 'official Air Force records documenting it are now held by AARO and the FBI', and reported that a witness was threatened and told to keep quiet. Wiggins testified to 15 February 2023, approximately 7:15 pm PST, aboard USS Jackson: four self-luminous Tic-Tac-shaped objects, one emerging from the ocean, holding formation and departing with near-instantaneous acceleration and no propulsion signature or sonic boom, recorded on the ship's Star SAFIRE multi-spectral EO/IR system with timestamped data and reported to the tactical action officer. Knapp gave the most detailed public account yet of AAWSAP and BAASS: prime contractor status, roughly fifty investigators with top secret clearances, 27 months of operation, three dozen preliminary reports, over a hundred research papers, a 240,000-case data warehouse designed by Jacques Vallee that reportedly remains in agency use, and the fact that most of the papers remain unreleased by DIA. He also described James Lacatski's 2023 statement to DHS that the United States possesses a craft of unknown origin whose interior had been accessed, and the incomplete Bigelow-Lockheed material negotiation. Borland described a summer 2012 triangular craft observation at Langley AFB, alleged more than a decade of retaliation including blacklisting and clearance-record manipulation, and stated he had filed complaints with AARO in March 2023 and the Intelligence Community Inspector General in August 2023. The committee's two findings are the ones that matter: agencies withheld information from the Task Force, and UAP-related spending flows to entities outside the reach of the Freedom of Information Act. That second finding is the direct antecedent of Rep. Burlison's FY2027 NDAA amendment adopted on 23 July 2026, which extends disclosure obligations to government contractors. As of 12 August 2026 this remains the most recent congressional hearing devoted to UAP.

timeline.label: White Sands Proving Ground established
timeline.text: Seven days before Trinity, the Army stands up the proving ground that will become the largest military installation in the United States and the geographic centre of the 1947-1951 New Mexico record.

timeline.label: Brazel reports the Foster Ranch debris
timeline.text: Mac Brazel reports the debris to Chaves County Sheriff George Wilcox, who calls Roswell Army Air Field. Maj. Jesse Marcel of the 509th Bomb Group and Capt. Sheridan Cavitt of the CIC are sent to retrieve it.

timeline.label: RAAF announces a disc, and takes it back the same day
timeline.text: 1st Lt. Walter Haut issues the 'flying disc' release; within hours Brig. Gen. Roger Ramey presents the material at Fort Worth as a weather balloon. The Air Force will concede in 1994 that the balloon statement was a cover story.

timeline.label: Wright-Patterson and Kirtland are both constituted
timeline.text: On the same day the Air Force formally establishes Wright-Patterson AFB, the address of foreign materiel exploitation, and Kirtland AFB, the nuclear weapons and directed energy complex inside Albuquerque.

timeline.label: Nuclear scientists meet at Los Alamos about the green fireballs
timeline.text: Edward Teller and Lincoln LaPaz attend a conference on the anomalous objects over northern New Mexico's nuclear installations. LANL's own account records the phenomenon was ultimately dismissed as a national security threat.

timeline.label: The CIA establishes the Groom Lake facility
timeline.text: Project AQUATONE selects the site because U-2 testing cannot be conducted at Edwards or Palmdale given the secrecy of the project. The first U-2 arrives 24 July 1955.

timeline.label: The conclusion is written before the study
timeline.text: Robert Low's memorandum proposes a study 'conducted almost entirely by non-believers' with 'almost zero expectation of finding a saucer'. McDonald finds it in the project files in July 1967.

timeline.label: Blue Book is terminated on the Condon findings
timeline.text: The Air Force closes its public reporting channel citing the University of Colorado report. The Bolender memo of the same period records that reports affecting national security were never in that channel.

timeline.label: SCANATE begins
timeline.text: The CIA initiates 'scan by coordinate' in response to assessments of Soviet psychotronic spending. SRI research under Puthoff and Targ follows in 1972.

timeline.label: HAVE BLUE flies at Groom Lake
timeline.text: Lockheed's stealth demonstrator first flies from a facility whose existence the government will not acknowledge for another twenty-one years.

timeline.label: Bennewitz begins his Manzano study
timeline.text: The Albuquerque businessman starts a self-funded study of lights and signals over the Kirtland/Manzano nuclear weapons storage area. He contacts the base 24 October 1980 and briefs officials 10 November 1980.

timeline.label: The F-117 moves to Tonopah
timeline.text: The 4450th Tactical Group relocates from Groom Lake to the Tonopah Test Range. A manned operational combat squadron will fly from a hidden base for six years before acknowledgement in November 1988.

timeline.label: Moore admits the Bennewitz deception
timeline.text: William Moore states publicly that he attempted to push Bennewitz toward a breakdown by feeding him false information. Bennewitz had been hospitalised in August 1988; he dies 23 June 2003.

timeline.label: Lazar goes on television in Las Vegas
timeline.text: George Knapp broadcasts the Robert Lazar interviews on KLAS-TV, creating the public reverse-engineering narrative attached to Area 51 and S-4. No primary record has ever corroborated it.

timeline.label: Groom Lake contractors sue
timeline.text: Kasza v. Browner and Frost v. Perry allege exposure to hazardous waste burned in open pits. Judge Philip Pro rejects the state secrets claim; the suits are dismissed for lack of evidence and the Ninth Circuit affirms.

timeline.label: The President exempts a place that officially does not exist
timeline.text: Clinton issues a determination exempting 'the Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake, Nevada' from environmental disclosure law - the only formal recognition to that date that Groom Lake is more than part of the Nellis complex. It is reissued annually.

timeline.label: GAO finds the Roswell records destroyed
timeline.text: GAO/NSIAD-95-187 reports that RAAF outgoing messages from October 1946 to December 1949 were destroyed with no disposition authority located. No agency has ever rebutted it.

timeline.label: STAR GATE is terminated
timeline.text: CIA's AIR evaluation finds remote viewing information 'vague and ambiguous' and unusable for actionable intelligence. The roughly $20 million programme ends; the records are published to CREST in January 2017.

timeline.label: Bigelow buys Skinwalker Ranch
timeline.text: Robert Bigelow purchases the 512-acre Uintah County property for $200,000 and directs NIDS at it. John B. Alexander and Colm Kelleher log close to 100 incidents without publishable evidence.

timeline.label: The Air Force concedes the site exists
timeline.text: Forty-three years after establishment, the USAF acknowledges the existence of the operating location at Groom Lake - without describing anything done there.

timeline.label: A red square over the missile defense sites
timeline.text: Boeing contractors at Vandenberg report a massive glowing red square hovering silently over two missile defense sites; security personnel the same night describe a rectangular craft larger than a football field. A witness a week later is threatened and told to keep quiet.

timeline.label: The Nimitz intercept
timeline.text: Princeton vectors two VFA-41 F/A-18Fs to a contact it has held on Aegis for two weeks. Fravor, Dietrich and their WSOs watch a 46-foot white object for about five minutes; it departs and reappears at the CAP point 60 miles away in under a minute. A follow-on sortie records FLIR1.

timeline.label: The Princeton data goes missing
timeline.text: Three Princeton crewmen in different divisions - Day, Voorhis and Turner - describe unidentified personnel coming aboard within roughly 48 hours and removing or ordering wiped the recording media. No FOIA release, visit log or message traffic has ever identified them.

timeline.label: The CIA names Area 51
timeline.text: Answering a 2005 FOIA request by Jeffrey Richelson of the National Security Archive, the CIA releases the U-2 and OXCART history and acknowledges specific activity at the site - fifty-eight years after establishment.

timeline.label: 'Glowing Auras and Black Money'
timeline.text: Cooper, Blumenthal and Kean reveal AATIP, the $22 million appropriation, Elizondo's resignation and the Navy videos. No new physical evidence; decisive institutional standing. Every subsequent official act follows from this date.

timeline.label: The Army signs for the material
timeline.text: GVSC Director Jeffery Langhout signs a CRADA with To The Stars Academy at Detroit Arsenal covering inertial mass reduction and metamaterial waveguides. The text is released 18 October; all twenty-nine emails of correspondence are later withheld in full.

timeline.label: The Department releases FLIR1
timeline.text: DoD authorises release of the three Navy videos, stating the phenomena 'remain characterized as unidentified' - the government authenticating the artefact and declining to explain it.

timeline.label: The Navy's own report on the Tic Tac surfaces
timeline.text: 72 range fouler reports posted to the Navy FOIA reading room include the 14 November 2004 incident: a 46-foot object with no nacelles, pylons or wings, and the disposition line 'Reporting terminated at 3rd Fleet, there was no process to share the reporting.'

timeline.label: Grusch, Fravor and Graves testify
timeline.text: The first congressional hearing at which a former intelligence officer testifies under oath to a multi-decade crash retrieval programme. No contractor is called and no document production is compelled.

timeline.label: Shellenberger publishes Immaculate Constellation
timeline.text: Public reports an alleged parent USAP consolidating UAP observations, sourced to a current or former US government official and confirmed to Shellenberger by a former intelligence community official.

timeline.label: A programme name enters the Congressional Record
timeline.text: Mace moves the twelve-page report into the record from the dais. Elizondo answers 'Yes' when asked whether the government has conducted secret UAP crash retrieval programs. Mace says certain individuals did not want the hearing to happen and does not name them.

timeline.label: The Task Force turns to the machinery
timeline.text: Nuccetelli, Wiggins, Knapp and Borland testify. The committee finds agencies withheld information and that UAP spending flows to entities outside FOIA reach. Nuccetelli names AARO and the FBI as custodians of Vandenberg records.

timeline.label: The Task Force's 2026 hearing is about MKULTRA
timeline.text: Kinzer and O'Neill testify on the CIA programme whose records a Director of Central Intelligence ordered destroyed. No UAP witness appears in 2026.

timeline.label: Eleven months, no UAP hearing
timeline.text: Between 9 September 2025 and 12 August 2026 - covering the February 2026 release directive, five PURSUE tranches, the late FY2025 annual report, the NDA waiver and the Burlison amendment - Congress holds no hearing on UAP.

timeline.text: No AARO annual report, statement for the record or PURSUE tranche has addressed a programme name entered into the Congressional Record on 13 November 2024. The Department's position remains 'no record'.

l-groom-lake.desc: Acknowledgement chronology, stated plainly because it is the board's benchmark: facility established April 1955; no acknowledgement of any kind 1955-1995; 1995 presidential determination exempting 'the Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake, Nevada' from environmental disclosure law, issued in the shadow of Kasza v. Browner and reissued annually; 1998 USAF acknowledgement that the site exists; 25 June 2013 CIA release of the U-2/OXCART history naming Area 51 and admitting specific activity, in response to a FOIA request filed in 2005 by Jeffrey T. Richelson of the National Security Archive. Fifty-eight years from establishment to specific acknowledgement, and the concession was compelled by a records request rather than volunteered. Any claim that a programme of this kind 'could not stay secret' has to be measured against this chronology.

nimitz-2004.desc: The confiscation question, separated carefully. Fravor testified under oath on 26 July 2023 that 'the incident was never investigated, none of my crew were ever questioned, tapes were never taken' - a statement about the aircrew and the squadron. Kevin Day, Gary Voorhis and Jason Turner, all USS Princeton crew in different divisions, have described in public interviews since 2018 that personnel who did not identify themselves came aboard within roughly 48 hours and removed or ordered wiped the ship's recording media. These are not necessarily contradictory: they concern different platforms and different data. What is documented is that the Navy has never produced Princeton sensor data for 14 November 2004, and that the Navy's own range fouler report says reporting 'terminated at 3rd Fleet, there was no process to share the reporting.' What is not documented, anywhere, is the identity of the personnel, the authority under which they acted, or any visit log, deck-log entry or message traffic recording the visit. The board grades the confiscation as tier 3 for that reason and considers it the single highest-value FOIA target in the modern aviator record.

immaculate-constellation.desc: The shape of the official response matters more than its content. The Department of Defense has said it has 'no record' of the programme - a records assertion, and the standard formulation used by an office without read-on to an unacknowledged compartment. It has not said the programme does not exist. Former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick has denied it, but he departed AARO in December 2023, eleven months before the report surfaced. AARO itself has never addressed the name in any published product: not the FY2024 annual report, not the FY2025 report delivered 21 July 2026, not any statement for the record, and not in any of the five PURSUE tranches published between 8 May and 7 August 2026. AARO's own declassification information paper of September 2025 concedes that it cannot declassify independently and must request review from originating offices - which is a structural explanation for why an office chartered to resolve anomalies would have nothing to say about a compartment it is not read into. The result is that a named alleged USAP has sat in the Congressional Record for twenty-one months without a written executive branch response of any kind.

l-kirtland.desc: The Bennewitz operation is the best-documented instance in the American record of counterintelligence resources being deployed against a private citizen over UAP-adjacent observations, and both principal participants have admitted it. William Moore stated publicly on 1 July 1989 that he had attempted to push Bennewitz into a mental breakdown by feeding him false information; AFOSI special agent Richard C. Doty has said he was tasked in the 1980s with hoaxing documents and feeding false information to UFO researchers including Bennewitz; and a 1992 article held in the CIA library names both men. The material fed to Bennewitz - underground bases, alien-government agreements, the Dulce mythos - became load-bearing folklore that has contaminated the field for four decades. The stimulus that started it, the lights and signals Bennewitz recorded over the Manzano nuclear weapons storage area in 1979-1980, has never received an official explanation.

gaps: THE TWELVE-PAGE DOCUMENT. The Immaculate Constellation report was entered into the Congressional Record on 13 November 2024 and appears in the hearing's Index of Documents, but no retrievable primary file at a stable public URL has been located. The GPO print of Serial No. 118-135 should contain it as a submitted document; obtaining the PDF of the submitted-materials section of CHRG-118hhrg57440 is the single highest-value next step for this domain.

THE DEPARTMENT'S WRITTEN RESPONSE TO IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION. No written DoD, OUSD(I&S) or AARO response exists in the public record. The 'no record' formulation is known only through press statements attributed to spokesperson Sue Gough. A FOIA request for any records search declaration, tasking memorandum or classification review conducted in response to the 13 November 2024 entry would establish whether one was ever done.

PRINCETON SENSOR DATA AND THE CONFISCATION. No FOIA release, visit log, deck-log entry, or message traffic has ever identified the personnel who allegedly boarded USS Princeton around 15-16 November 2004, or the authority under which they acted. The Navy has never produced Princeton SPY-1B or CEC data for 14 November 2004. Targets: Princeton deck logs for 14-18 November 2004, CSG-11 message traffic, and the Third Fleet reporting file referenced in the range fouler report.

THE VANDENBERG RECORDS. Nuccetelli testified on 9 September 2025 that 'official Air Force records documenting it are now held by AARO and the FBI' for the 14 October 2003 and 2005 incidents. This is a named-custodian claim for specific dated incidents at a named installation. No FOIA production from either custodian has surfaced, and Congress has not compelled one.

WRIGHT-PATTERSON T-2 FILES, 1947-1951. The Air Materiel Command T-2 intelligence series at Wright Field for 1947-1951 has never been the subject of an identified comprehensive declassification review or NARA accession. If a legacy exploitation effort existed, this is where its earliest paper would sit. No finding aid has been located.

AAWSAP/BAASS RESEARCH PAPERS. Knapp testified that BAASS produced more than three dozen preliminary reports and over 100 detailed research papers, most of which DIA has never released, plus a 240,000-case data warehouse that reportedly remains in agency use. The DIRD series is partly public; the BAASS papers and the warehouse itself are not. Custody of the warehouse - which agency, under what contract - is unestablished.

GVSC/TTSA CORRESPONDENCE. Twenty-nine emails totalling one hundred pages of Dr. Joseph Cannon's correspondence with To The Stars Academy were located and withheld in full under FOIA exemptions (b)(4) and (b)(5). No characterisation results from the CRADA have ever been published. An exemption challenge or a congressional document demand is the route.

NO 2026 UAP HEARING. Between 9 September 2025 and 12 August 2026 no congressional hearing on UAP was held, despite the February 2026 presidential release directive, five PURSUE tranches, the late FY2025 AARO annual report, the July 2026 NDA waiver directive and the Burlison FY2027 NDAA amendment. Whether one is scheduled for the remainder of the 119th Congress, and whether the Task Force's remit survives, is unresolved.

THE SCHRIEVER PROVENANCE CLAIM. The 2025 assertion that Immaculate Constellation material came from a folder labelled '2018 Schriever Wargame' is attributed to an unnamed self-identified whistleblower and assessed by Jason Colavito as a misidentification. The claimant's identity, the underlying folder, and whether this claimant is Shellenberger's source or a separate later party are all unestablished. The board notes the claim addresses a later provenance story, not Shellenberger's sourcing.

PROJECT TWINKLE AND THE LAND-AIR OBSERVATIONS. The cinetheodolite tracking-camera observations from White Sands Proving Ground in 1948-1951 and the full Project Twinkle case file were not retrieved from a primary archive in this pass. The instrumented character of these observations makes them the most technically evaluable material in the legacy record.

HANGAR 18. No primary record establishes storage of Roswell or any other recovered material at Wright-Patterson Area B. The claim is recorded as folklore; the structural point about NASIC's continuous custody of the ATIC/FTD filing system stands independently and does not depend on it.

JANET AND THE GROOM WORKFORCE. The contractor of record, headcount and contract vehicle for the Las Vegas-Groom Lake air shuttle are unpublished. Establishing the size of the commuting workforce would put a hard number on the scale of population that has demonstrably kept a compartmented programme quiet.
